items.title: Google fined US$463 million for breaching EU rule on location data
items.description: Google has been fined 403 million euros (US$463 million) for breaching the European Union’s strict privacy rules because it mishandled users’ location data, the bloc’s data privacy watchdog said Monday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A sign is displayed on a Google building at their campus in Mountain View, Calif., Sept. 24, 2019. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Google has been fined 403 million euros (US$463 million) for breaching the European Union’s strict privacy rules because it mishandled users’ location data, the bloc’s data privacy watchdog said Monday.
items.body:
Google has been fined 403 million euros (US$463 million) for breaching the European Union’s strict privacy rules because it mishandled users’ location data, the bloc’s data privacy watchdog said Monday.

Ireland’s Data Protection Commission said its investigation found Google did not lawfully or fairly process location data in users’ Web & App Activity, a Google setting that tracks browsing and search history, and in their Location History, a service that maps places they’ve been with their mobile phones.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Regulators also found the company failed to be lawful, fair and transparent when it processed personal data in its Location Accuracy feature in the Android mobile operating system.

Ireland is the lead regulator for Google in the 27-nation EU because the U.S. tech giant’s European headquarters is based in Dublin.

The investigation, which opened six years ago, examined how Google applied the EU privacy rule book, known as the General Data Protection Regulation, from the time it took effect in 2018 until February 2020.

“This case centers around historical policies that have since been updated,” Google said in a statement. ”From 2019 onwards, we’ve significantly evolved our practices and launched robust tools that make managing location data simple.”

Regulators said that location data is a type of personal data that’s collected by Google and can be used to infer someone’s location.

“Location data can bring both benefits and harms to individuals,” Deputy Commissioner Graham Doyle said. “It can greatly enhance the utility of online services, but it can also reveal a significant amount of information about an individual, including information that is inherently private.”

It’s the fourth biggest EU privacy fine issued by the Irish watchdog, which has previously handed out bigger fines to TikTok and Meta, including a 1.2 billion euro fine for Meta.

The regulator said it still has three other ongoing privacy investigations involving Google.

The Associated Press

items.title: Carney misses UN event, Lametti steps in to make the case for multilateralism
items.description: Canada’s Representative to the United Nations made the case for multilateralism after Prime Minister Mark Carney missed the event at the General Assembly on Monday.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at a joint news conference with Prime Minister of Norway Jonas Gahr Store on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Patrick Doyle]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">PATRICK DOYLE</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Canada’s Representative to the United Nations made the case for multilateralism after Prime Minister Mark Carney missed the event at the General Assembly on Monday.
items.body:
UNITED NATIONS — Canada’s Representative to the United Nations made the case for multilateralism after Prime Minister Mark Carney missed the event at the General Assembly on Monday because of technical problems at a key regional air traffic control centre that halted operations at every major airport in the New York City area.

Hundreds of flights were cancelled in the U.S. northeast after a key circuit failed at an air traffic facility in Philadelphia. The Prime Minister’s Office said Carney arrived in New York City later Monday night.

Canada’s Ambassador to the United Nations David Lametti spoke in Carney’s place during a roundtable discussion on strengthening multilateral collaboration with European Council President António Costa and Kenya’s President William Ruto on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The discussion took place at the Partners for Multilateralism summit, or P4M, a gathering of leaders to discuss coalition-building and translating shared principles into practical action.

Lametti said Carney has spoke about the “rupture” the world is living through — referencing the prime minister’s widely applauded speech in Davos earlier this year — but now it is time to talk about what’s next.

He said coalitions of the willing must come together to deal with specific issues and find ways to actionable results. Lametti said nations ready to act should “build trust and prove what works” and then bring it back to the larger multilateralism structure.

Carney, Costa, Ruto and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva co-wrote an opinion piece published Sunday in The Financial Times that argues the global community is more interdependent than ever, “even as it becomes more fragmented and polarized.”

They pointed to climate change, global pandemics, financial shocks, conflicts and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz as global crises that require countries to work together.

“Cooperation is therefore not an act of idealism, it is a practical necessity,” the leaders wrote. “The question is not whether multilateralism can survive, but how it must evolve to meet the realities of our time.”

Trump’s return to the White House and his unpredictable tariff campaign have upended global institutions and pushed away traditional allies.

Trump and members of his administration have demanded significant changes to the UN and have held back funding for the institution, putting it in turmoil.

Brazil’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Mauro Vieira didn’t mention Trump by name but said there are nations who want to make the world into spheres of influence, language used by the current U.S. administration.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese talked about middle power countries that need to come together, “stepping up and being outward looking.”

As Trump looks to realign the global order, Carney has emerged in the role of coalition builder — something that appears to irritate the president. Earlier Monday, Trump posted on social media that the United States is working on a “massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus.”

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” Trump said.

Details of that proposed deal remain unclear. It’s the latest shot Trump has taken at Canada since trade talks broke down in acrimony last month.

On Bloomberg Television on Monday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer again accused Canada of ending the trade talks and claimed the escalating tariff war won’t have much of an impact on the U.S. economy.

Greer said Canada now wants to “get together” with the European Union. That’s a reference to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen using her state of the union address to the European Parliament last week to open the door to Canada becoming what she called the first “associate member.”

“They’ve been very clear over the past year and a half, they’re sovereign. They may want to tie up with the EU now so it raises the question of that whole sovereignty shtick,” Greer said.

Trump is set to give a speech in front of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday. Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is set to deliver a speech to the General Assembly later in the week.

Carney, who is scheduled to be in New York City from Monday to Wednesday, is still expected to attend a discussion on the two-state solution in the Middle East on Tuesday and meet with global and business leaders on the sidelines of the event.

For nearly a year now, Carney has been promoting the idea of bringing countries around the world together to pursue what he has called “shared interests, and occasionally shared values, rather than shared institutions.”

Carney has sought to build a bridge between the EU and a Pacific Rim trading bloc called CPTPP so that middle powers can better resist economic coercion by the U.S. and China.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

- With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa

items.title: Parliament returns with some new MPs, more vacant seats and a major economic bill
items.description: Members of Parliament returned from their summer break Monday with trade tensions hanging over the country, a new but undefined alliance with Europe on the horizon, and a Liberal government ready to push an aggressive agenda to get major new infrastructure approved.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A House of Commons maintenance and material handling employee wipes down the Speakers chair in the House of Commons during a photo op in Ottawa, Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Members of Parliament returned from their summer break Monday with trade tensions hanging over the country, a new but undefined alliance with Europe on the horizon, and a Liberal government ready to push an aggressive agenda to get major new infrastructure approved.
items.body:
OTTAWA -- The governing Liberals used their first day back from summer break to introduce a new bill to speed up the construction of infrastructure projects as trade tensions with the U.S. hang over the country.

Buoyed by strong polling numbers and three recent byelection wins that narrowly expanded their governing majority, Prime Minister Mark Carney and his caucus began the fall sitting by introducing the Building Canada Strong Act.

The Liberals said the new Bill C-39, introduced Monday after question period, is aimed at speeding up approvals for major projects.

The legislation landed not long after Carney hosted an international investment summit that sought billions of dollars for infrastructure across the country, including data centres, ports, airports and energy projects.

The proposed law would also make substantial changes to a controversial provision of the Canada Labour Code.

Union leaders warned it could weaken the right to strike. Labour Minister Patty Hajdu strongly rejected that characterization of the bill on Monday.

Carney’s government presented the legislation as another step in its campaign to shore up the economy and make it less reliant on the United States through new trade avenues to Europe and Asia.

The bill is sure to dominate much of the debate in the House of Commons this fall.

Monday’s question period began with Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre calling on Carney to stand with him in support of the Jewish community and an injured police officer following a shooting at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., on Sunday during Yom Kippur.

Carney replied there is no place for hate of any kind in Canada.

Shortly after that, the usual partisan tone returned as the federal parties sparred over Canada’s affordability crisis.

Poilievre picked up where he left off before the break, arguing government polices are driving inflation and saying grocery prices have reached “insane” levels.

He said Canadians can’t “eat speeches, summits or signing ceremonies.”

The prime minister pointed to three wars affecting Canadians right now: the trade war with the Americans, the U.S. war with Iran and Russia’s war on Ukraine.

“They are pushing up fuel prices. They are pushing up grocery prices. So we are providing immediate support to Canadians,” Carney said, pointing to the groceries and essentials benefit.

The prime minister said the government is working “tooth-and-nail to make Canadians’ lives more affordable.”

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne on Monday introduced a new bill to extend the excise tax break on fuel. The government promised the move earlier this month.

The first order of business for the House of Commons on Monday was for Speaker Francis Scarpaleggia to read off the list of seats which have become vacant in recent months.

Since the House rose for the summer in mid-June, nine MPs have stepped down.

Three byelections have already have been held, which the Liberals swept. The governing party easily held ridings in Toronto and North Vancouver and snatched a seat away from the Conservatives in Quebec.

Carney was all smiles Monday as he accompanied his three new MPs into the House for the first time: his former deputy chief of staff Braeden Caley from North Vancouver-Capilano, former political staffer Tanveer Shahnawaz from Beaches-East York, and dairy farmer Daniel Gobeil from Chicoutimi-Le Fjord.

The six remaining vacant seats will require byelections in the coming months. They include two seats previously held by the Liberals, two previously held by the Conservatives and one each held by the Bloc Québécois and NDP after the last election.

The trade tensions with the United States will be a dominant theme of the fall sitting, as President Donald Trump’s White House cranks up the pressure on Canada and threatens its sovereignty. 

Trump has threatened to escalate his deepening trade war with additional tariffs on steel and autos if the two sides can’t reach an agreement by the end of the year.

Canada’s negotiating team walked away from the trade talks in August at the 11th hour, saying it was a bad deal for Canada.

The trade conflict then escalated, with Trump imposing another volley of tariffs while Canada imposed its own counter-tariffs. 

Trump also attempted to rebrand Lake Ontario as Lake America and sought to cut off certain Canadian imports to the United States.

Carney responded by stepping up his efforts to deepen Canada’s ties elsewhere. In a speech to the European Parliament last week, Carney welcomed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s move to work on making Canada an associate member of the European Union.

What that status would mean has yet to be determined. More detail is expected to come out of a Canada-Europe summit in Montreal in October.

Carney met over the weekend with French President Emmanuel Macron in St-Pierre-Miquelon, France’s archipelago territory just off the coast of Newfoundland, and with Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Ottawa.

Carney will be in New York for meetings at the United Nations this week, though he is not scheduled to address the General Assembly.

The prime minister is expected to have more travel over the fall months, with several summits on the horizon.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

David Baxter with files Kyle Duggan and Craig Lord

items.title: Ontario real estate investors in limbo as ‘Simple Investor’ property firm suspends payments
items.description: Hundreds of real estate investors in a company run by a media-savvy realtor that owns dozens of buildings across Ontario got a shock over the weekend when they were told their rent payments are in limbo.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Todd C. Slater, next to a "Simple Company" sign. (Jon Woodward)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: Hundreds of real estate investors in a company run by a media-savvy realtor that owns dozens of buildings across Ontario got a shock over the weekend when they were told their rent payments are in limbo.
items.body:
Hundreds of real estate investors in a company run by a media-savvy realtor who owns dozens of buildings across Ontario got a shock over the weekend when they were told their rent payments were in limbo.

The realtor, Todd C. Slater, is known as the Simple Investor through advertising, a radio show he once hosted on Newstalk 1010 and a series of podcasts.

Now, however, the condo management company, estimated to be worth more than $100 million, seems to be anything but simple.

“We put a lot of trust in Todd, and I trusted him for a long time. We trusted him for a long time. That trust is gone, obviously,” said Billie-Jo Newman, an investor who owns six properties in four Ontario cities through Slater’s company, The Simple Investor.

Newman said she got good returns for 13 years from a company whose business model was to buy apartment buildings, turn them into condos, sell the condos and provide a hands-off investment for the owners by managing the properties for a fee.

In January, however, she said she was confused when she got a $41,000 water bill for a condo complex in Perth County.

Then, she said, there was a change in payment deadlines, a $100 increase in the per-condo management fee and, this month, her rent money didn’t come in at all, putting her ability to make mortgage payments in doubt.

“I’m trying to look at this in steps, because if I look at the whole thing it’s very overwhelming,” Newman said.

Sireg, the company that manages the Simple Investor properties, told investors in a letter last week that it’s working on solutions.

“The Company is currently experiencing market and liquidity challenges that are affecting our ability to make timely rental payments. We recognize how serious this is, particularly for investors who rely on these payments to meet financial obligations. The Company is working with advisors to evaluate alternatives and address these challenges,” the letter says.

The company didn’t respond to emails from CTV News, and when CTV News reached out to Slater directly, an automated email said, “I am away on medical leave with no date of return at this time.”

Some buildings managed by Sireg have had problems, with one complex on Kipps Lane in London without hot water for a period of time this summer and another building in Brockville without a working elevator.

Investor Marcin Migdal, operator of AiCanadianSolutions.ca, said he panicked when he realized the payments would not be coming in. He later started a website to organize investors with SIREG and Simple Investor.

He said he has already heard from more than 79 investors with some $26 million in assets. He said he had heard there are approximately 1,800 total investors.

“I didn’t want to sit around and wait. So I just sprang into action to rally other investors and try to get to the bottom of what is happening with Todd,” Migdal said in an interview, recalling that he met Slater many times and calling him a “very nice person.”

Migdal said he isn’t sure what has happened, but wondered if Slater overextended himself in real estate during a period of contraction in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic and a downturn in condo values in Toronto.

The condo ownership has not changed, and the tenants are likely still paying rent. But one challenge for the owners is that, because the investment was so hands-off, many don’t have contact information to reach the tenants.

He said the first piece of advice he has for worried investors is that they can call their bank and ask to defer their mortgage for a few months. Investors will still be paying interest, but without paying the principal, their payments will be reduced, he said.

items.title: Carney says he won't backtrack on digital services tax, streamers' CanCon payments
items.description: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he won’t change his mind about his decision to eliminate the digital services tax and Canadian content contributions for streamers.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Prime Minister Mark Carney rises during question period on Parliament Hill in Ottawa on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Adrian Wyld]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Adrian Wyld</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he won’t change his mind about his decision to eliminate the digital services tax and Canadian content contributions for streamers.
items.body:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he won’t change his mind about his decision to eliminate the digital services tax and Canadian content contributions for streamers.

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet asked Carney in the House of Commons on Monday whether he would reconsider those decisions, since they failed to secure progress in trade talks with the United States.

“No,” Carney replied.

Blanchet said in French that Carney’s strategy failed and that big tech companies, whose revenue streams are larger than those of some countries, should have to contribute to arts and culture.

Carney responded that it was the Americans who failed to put in place restrictions on the French language and Canadian culture.

Carney said last month the U.S. put pressure on Canada to adjust its position on the rules around discoverability of content online. He said those U.S. demands would have affected Canada’s ability to protect its culture, including the French language.

He cited that as one of the reasons his government ended negotiations in August.

Those discoverability rules, which are not yet in place, are enabled by the Online Steaming Act.

The CRTC previously said that, under that legislation, it would require large streaming services like Netflix to contribute 15 per cent of their Canadian revenues to support Canadian content.

The government said in June it would eliminate the financial contribution requirement, though it has not yet officially started that process.

The digital services tax was a separate government measure that would have imposed a three-per-cent levy on revenue from Canadian users on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Uber and Airbnb.

Just before the first payment was due last year, Carney said he would eliminate the tax in order to restart trade talks with the United States.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

items.title: Liberals table bill to speed up major projects, labour groups voice concerns about impact on strike action
items.description: On their first day back in the House of Commons after a three-month summer hiatus, the Liberals on Monday tabled a significant piece of legislation aimed at speeding up major project approvals, though it’s already raising concerns among labour groups.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[The House of Commons and Containers being unloaded from a container ship at Deltaport, at Roberts Bank in Delta, B.C., in a combination photo. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Darryl Dyck]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: On their first day back in the House of Commons after a three-month summer hiatus, the Liberals on Monday tabled a significant piece of legislation aimed at speeding up major project approvals, though it’s already raising concerns among labour groups.
items.body:
OTTAWA — On their first day back in the House of Commons after a three-month summer hiatus, the Liberals on Monday tabled a significant piece of legislation aimed at speeding up major project approvals, though it’s already raising concerns among labour groups.

Bill C-39 — dubbed the Building Canada Strong Act by the Liberals — is meant to accelerate review and approval times for major projects to get them built quicker.

The announcement Monday was made by Government House leader Steven MacKinnon, Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu, and Dominic LeBlanc, the minister for intergovernmental affairs and One Canadian Economy, and minister of internal trade.

This fall sitting’s first piece of legislation comes on the heels of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s inaugural investment summit last week, which pitched dozens of foreign investors on more than 150 Canadian infrastructure projects, with the goal of courting $1 trillion in funding.

“This will give business the confidence to invest in Canada, accelerate projects, and drive long-term growth and prosperity that protects the environment and upholds Indigenous rights,” reads a statement from the federal government about C-39, which it categorizes as “the most comprehensive and ambitious reform to Canada’s ability to get big things built in a generation.”

“It will reshape the regulatory approvals process, maintain Canada’s rigorous standards and uphold Indigenous rights,” the statement reads.

Labour groups ‘watching closely’

But, labour groups say they’re concerned changes to the Canada Labour Code included in the bill will have adverse consequences for workers and strip them of their right to strike.

The new legislation is built on three pillars, according to the federal government: build Canada now, keep Canada moving, and Canada strong for all.

It’s under the latter pillar that the government is proposing changes to the Labour Code, pledging to “strengthen collective bargaining by helping parties address issues earlier, reach negotiated agreements, and resolve disputes while fully protecting the right to strike.”

Specifically, according to a senior government official speaking to reporters during a technical briefing ahead of the official announcement, the changes will largely affect the collective bargaining process for industries that have previously seen strike action or imposed mediation.

In a statement Monday, Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske wrote that “Canada’s unions will be watching (C-39) closely.”

“The government has repeatedly said it will protect the right to strike,” Bruske also wrote. “We welcome that commitment. Today, we expect to see what it means in practice.”

Bruske then referenced the protracted and ongoing trade war with the United States.

“Canada’s unions are part of Team Canada,” she wrote. “We have our elbows up. We are ready to build, invest and fight for Canadian jobs. But we can’t have our elbows up against (U.S. President Donald) Trump with our hands tied at the bargaining table.”

Bruske said unions will review with legislation carefully and respond once they’ve done so, but added any restriction on workers’ right to strike is “unacceptable.”

Addressing his caucus last week, Carney called the fall sitting of Parliament a “crucial” one, and promised the Liberals are “going to introduce some of the most consequential legislation, not just of this government, but in decades” in the coming months.

Helping them to get legislation passed, the Liberals currently hold a majority government, after months of floor crossing, resignations, and now two rounds of by-elections.

Asked about the proposed changes to the Labour Code, Conservative House leader Andrew Scheer said in an interview on CTV Power Play with Vassy Kapelos that his party’s labour critic would respond once they’ve had time to read the bill thoroughly.

NDP Leader Avi Lewis, meanwhile, held a press conference on Parliament Hill following the ministers’ announcement, saying he believes the legislation is consequential enough that he is “breaking (his) silence” on Yom Kippur.

“Prime Minister Carney is using our fear and disorientation around the trade war to push through a series of unpopular measures that he did not run on, has no mandate for, and would never get away with under normal circumstances,” Lewis said.

With files from CTV News’ Vassy Kapelos, Judy Trinh, Rachel Aiello and Samantha Pope

items.title: ‘Blood potash’: Scott Moe reacts to Trump’s Belarus deal
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[This combination photos shows potash and U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday Sept. 18, 2026. (AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.
items.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump says he is working on a “massive deal” to purchase potash from Belarus.

“The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers,” he posted to Truth Social on Monday.

Canada is the leading exporter of potash, shipping about 22.9 million tonnes in 2024, accounting for over 39 per cent of global exports according to the Government of Canada.

The leading destination of Canadian exports of potash is the United States. The U.S. imports nearly 85 per cent of its potash from Canada.

Belarus ranks third in potash production behind Russia and Canada.

According to Belarusian media reports Monday, President Alexander Lukashenko said even if there was a desire to enter western markets, there is nothing left to supply.

According to reporting from Reuters, potash from Belarus remains under EU sanctions, and the landlocked country has been barred from exporting via the Lithuanian port of Klaipeda since February 2022.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe, whose province provides the U.S. with more than 86 per cent of its potash supply from Canada, said Trump’s tentative deal is “wrong and it doesn’t make sense.”

“More than 40 countries - Canada and its allies - have sanctions against Belarus for supporting war criminal Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. Buying blood potash from Belarus is supporting Russian aggression” he posted to X Monday afternoon.

“Does anyone believe Belarusian blood potash shipped through Russia is going to be more affordable, more sustainable or more ethical than potash shipped from Saskatchewan - right here in North America?”

Potash leverage in U.S.-Canada trade war

In June, Trump told reporters that there is nothing the U.S. needs from Canada. However, U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra said America needs a “tremendous amount of things” including Canadian potash, since there are “not lots of other places that you can get it.”

Canada’s premiers have been at odds about whether to leverage the critical mineral against the U.S. amid trade war tensions.

While Ontario Premier Doug Ford has previously pushed to retaliate against Trump’s tariffs by cutting U.S. access to electricity, oil and other minerals, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Moe said they were concerned about the long-term consequences for those industries.

Canada’s 10 active potash mines are located in Saskatchewan.

Moe has said the province would not support any kind of export taxes or withholding supply for the U.S., as losing its biggest customer would cause job losses, price hikes and a tremendous hit to the local economy.

“The United States of America, most assuredly, would switch to buying potash from other nations around the world. We would lose a long-term customer to some degree,” Moe said during trade talks.

Smith also echoed Moe in July, when she told reporters oil and potash being used as retaliatory measures is “not going to happen.”

Canadian potash has remained exempt from Trump’s tariffs amid the ongoing trade war. However, the U.S. looking to Belarus for potash supply signifies the latest escalation.

The move comes after Prime Minister Mark Carney welcomed the “ambition” to become the European Union’s first associate member, which Trump said he’ll retaliate against if he deems it to be a “hostile act.”

Belarus sanctions

The U.S., Canada and EU have all imposed sanctions on Belarus for its crackdown on human rights and for allowing its territory to be used by Russia for its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

However, in December 2025, the U.S. agreed to lift sanctions on Belarusian potash, after Lukashenko freed 123 prisoners with the help of Trump’s envoy.

With files from The Canadian Press

items.title: Ontario halves eviction notice period under new rental rules
items.description: Ontario's new rental rules take effect today — here's what it means for broker clients
items.content: <p>Ontario's new rental rules take effect today — here's what it means for broker clients</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639256179236082597.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Ontario's new rental rules take effect today — here's what it means for broker clients
items.body:
A second wave of amendments to Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act (RTA) took effect on September 21, cutting the repayment window for tenants in arrears in half and reshaping the terms that govern rental investments across the province.

The changes — drawn from Bill 60 and Bill 97 — follow an initial round of RTA reforms that came into force in July.

For mortgage brokers with investor clients in Ontario, the new frameworkaffects cash flow assumptions, rental income qualification, and the regulatory risk profile of mortgage-backed rental properties.

Key changes brokers and their investor clients should know

The most significant amendments under Bill 60 and Bill 97 are as follows:

  • The N4 notice repayment window is cut from 14 days to seven. If payment is not received within that window, the landlord can file an L1 application with the Landlord and Tenant Board (LTB) to commence eviction proceedings.
  • "Persistent late payment" now has a statutory definition for the first time: rent paid more than seven days after the due date on at least three separate occasions within a six-month period, giving landlords a clearer legal threshold to document habitual delays.
  • A landlord issuing an N12 notice for personal or family use with at least 120 days of advance notice is no longer required to pay the tenant compensation, though if the intended occupant does not move in within 60 days, the eviction is presumed to be in bad faith.
  • Tenants who wish to raise separate complaints at an eviction hearing, such as maintenance failures or landlord harassment, must now pay 50% of the alleged overdue rent before those issues can be introduced.

A tighter market adds urgency for landlord investors

The RTA changes land as Ontario's investment property sector faces compound headwinds.

Canadian Mortgage Professional has reported on how a sharp population decline is reshaping Canada's rental and condo markets} and on how unsold new condo inventory in the Greater Toronto Hamilton Area hit a 35-year low in the first quarter of 2026.

Toronto-area broker Micky Khaneka of MKG Mortgages told CMP that the challenges facing Toronto's condo marketsuggest it "might be a little bit longer before that starts to be absorbed."

A rental market report by Rentals.ca and Urbanation for August placed the asking rent to $2,035, with apartment and condo rents in Toronto rising 1.6% from June to $2,577. 

For brokers advising rental investor clients in Ontario, the new LTB timelines and eviction thresholds are an increasingly relevant factor in the due diligence conversation around mortgage-backed rental holdings in the province.

items.title: Bank of Canada governor flags growth risk as tariff talks break down
items.description: Tiff Macklem says fresh trade tensions and rising oil prices cloud Canada's economic outlook
items.content: <p>Tiff Macklem says fresh trade tensions and rising oil prices cloud Canada's economic outlook</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639256168711399271.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Tiff Macklem says fresh trade tensions and rising oil prices cloud Canada's economic outlook
items.body:
Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem issued a stark warning Monday that a fresh round of US tariffs and elevated global oil prices risk undoing Canada's hard-won economic recovery.

Speaking at the Halifax Partnership in Nova Scotia on September 21, Macklem said the economy had entered the summer on solid footing.

Non-energy exports rose 14.5% on an annualized basis in the second quarter of 2026, their highest level since early 2025. Business investment, meanwhile, climbed 8.8% over the same period.

Companies had adjusted supply chains and diversified export relationships, reducing dependence on the US market.

"Taken together, these developments suggest the economy entered the summer in a stronger position," Macklem said.

"Growth had resumed, investment was picking up and companies were beginning to look beyond the headwinds to opportunity."

Trade and energy pressures test Canada's economic rebound

That momentum now faces pressure from two directions. For brokers tracking how US tariff escalation is reshaping the Bank of Canada's rate path, the breakdown in Canada-US trade negotiations signals another potential pause in business investment and hiring.

If the latest duties remain in place, the Bank estimates fourth-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) growth could be roughly halved to below 1%. The affected goods represent approximately 5% of Canada's exports to the United States.

The Middle East conflict adds a second constraint. Damage to global refining capacity has driven gasoline and diesel prices higher, keeping consumer price index (CPI) inflation near 3% for several months.

If global oil prices hold near US$100 per barrel, the Bank expects inflation to edge further above target.

"The developments are pulling the economy in different directions," Macklem said.

"One creates downside risks to growth, while the other creates upside risks to inflation."

The latest Bank of Canada minutes show growing concern about energy prices, inflation risks, and trade uncertainty. Tiff Macklem of the Bank of Canada and Leslie Preston of TD Economics weigh in on the outlook.https://t.co/7EBVbT9OBI — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 18, 2026

What the rate hold means for mortgage brokers

Brokers will recall similar warnings about persistent energy inflation triggering rate hikes. CMP's reporting on whether economists now see rates heading higher sooner than expected found divergence after September 2's hold at 2.25%.

Philip Petursson, chief investment strategist at IG Wealth Management in Canada, placed the next rate hike no earlier than 2027.

Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics, suggested "an interest rate hike at the final meeting of the year, in December, is arguably now looking more likely" if energy prices persist.

Macklem was clear that monetary policy has limits. The central bank cannot offset tariff effects or control global energy prices.

"As these risks evolve, we are prepared to adjust monetary policy as needed," he said.

"We remain focused on keeping inflation low, stable and predictable. In an uncertain world, that's one of the most important contributions we can make to the economic well-being of all Canadians."

The Bank will introduce a new forecasting model called Prima for its October Monetary Policy Report, designed to better distinguish temporary inflation pressures from persistent ones.

items.title: The home types driving Ottawa's new build surge
items.description: One property type is pulling buyers off the sidelines in Ottawa's new home market
items.content: <p>One property type is pulling buyers off the sidelines in Ottawa's new home market</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639256149883977184.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: One property type is pulling buyers off the sidelines in Ottawa's new home market
items.body:
Ottawa's new home market extended its strong run in August, recording 464 sales. That's a 55.2% jump from the 299 homes sold in the same month a year earlier. The figures come from the Greater Ottawa Home Builders' Association (GOHBA) and PMA Brethour Realty Group.

Month-over-month, sales climbed 9.7% from July's 423 transactions.

Year-to-date new home sales in Ottawa now stand at 3,557, a 50.4% increase over the 2,365 recorded through the first eight months of 2025.

Townhomes led all product types, claiming 46% of sales. Condo townhomes surged to 19% from 8% in July.

Single-detached homes accounted for 34% while condo apartments made up the remaining 1%.

Affordability shaping what buyers choose

Jason Burggraaf, Executive Director of the Greater Ottawa Home Builders' Association, said the product mix reflects how budget constraints are directing buyer decisions in the capital.

"August's sales show that demand for new homes remains strong, but affordability is clearly shaping what buyers choose," Burggraaf said.

"With townhomes and condominium townhomes making up well over half of sales, buyers are gravitating toward more attainable housing options. Governments need to ensure that the way we fund growth doesn't add costs that put those homes further out of reach."

Burggraaf's warning about the cost of funding growth speaks directly to development charges, a persistent pressure point for Ontario builders.

In GTA municipalities, those charges can exceed $100,000 on a new single-family home, according to a C.D. Howe Institute analysis published in 2026.

https://www.gohba.ca/2026/09/21/gohba-pma-brethour-ottawa-new-home-sales-report-august2026/A joint federal-provincial commitment to reduce development charges by up to 50% is working through the pipeline alongside Ontario's move to scrap the HST on new homes in a one-year push}, which offers eligible buyers a rebate of up to $130,000 on homes valued up to $1 million. That program runs until March 31, 2027.

West Ottawa leads the geographic split

The western portion of the city dominated August activity, capturing 40% of new home sales. The south followed at 36%, the east at 20%, and Central Ottawa at 5%.

The results land against a national backdrop that is improving but fragile. Canada's housing affordability reached a four-year best in Q1 2026, according to RBC Economics, with the national aggregate measure falling to 53% of pre-tax median household income required to cover ownership costs.

Yet the pace of gains is narrowing. CMHC has warned that a slowdown in new construction could reverse recent affordability progress if Canada underbuilds through the current soft patch in the market.

items.title: Lululemon, Canada Goose and Ikea, among brands expanding into resale markets
items.description: As Canadians increasingly turn to second-hand goods to stretch their dollars, some of the country’s biggest brands are looking to capture a piece of the growing resale market themselves.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Canada Goose, IKEA and Lululemon brands.]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: As Canadians increasingly turn to second-hand goods to stretch their dollars, some of the country’s biggest brands are looking to capture a piece of the growing resale market themselves.
items.body:
CALGARY - As Canadians increasingly turn to second-hand goods to stretch their dollars, some of the country’s biggest brands are looking to capture a piece of the growing resale market themselves.

Vancouver-based Lululemon is among the companies expanding into resale in Canada - joining brands including Canada Goose and Ikea - that are giving customers ways to sell back used products so they can be resold to someone else.

“Their products are already being sold in the resale market. Why not just enter that market, control the image, the presentation of that product and acquire new customers along the way?” said Sid Mookerjee, an assistant professor of marketing at McGill University.

Mookerjee said brands see an opportunity to reach consumers who may want their products but aren’t willing or able to pay full price.

The shift comes as traditional thrift and consignment stores are also seeing growing interest from shoppers.

Lea Wilhelm, owner of Calgary’s The Peacock Boutique Consignment, said the consignment business has been around for 50 years and sells a range of high-end brands, including Lululemon.

“I think people are becoming a little more conscious of their spending,” she said. “People still want good quality. So businesses like ours can provide good quality for a fraction of the cost.”

She said she welcomes major retailers extending the life of their products and isn’t worried about the added competition.

Peacock can pay consignors cash rather than limiting compensation to store credit, she said. The store also carries products from numerous brands.

“We’ve differentiated enough that we’re not solely dependent on one brand or style or whatnot to resell to our customers.”

Resale popularity booms

The growth of resale is also creating another business opportunity: the infrastructure needed to get millions of used products ready to be sold again.

Lululemon expanded its Like New resale program into Canada earlier this year through a partnership with Denver-based Tersus Solutions, a company that handles the behind-the-scenes work of putting used products back on the market.

Under the program, customers can trade in clean, gently used Lululemon items that meet the company’s eligibility requirements in exchange for an electronic gift card that can be used online or in stores.

Lululemon did not respond to requests for an interview.

Every item sold through the Canadian program passes through Tersus’s new 25,000-square-foot Calgary facility, its first outside the United States. There, items are cleaned and assessed, photographed and listed online, before being packed and shipped to their next owner.

“We’ve had many, many days where we’re shipping more than a thousand pieces out of product that’s come in, being put through the system of recommerce and consumers are buying them back for, as Lulu would say, for their second win,” said Steve Bommer, general manager for Tersus Canada.

Tersus uses pressurized carbon dioxide rather than water to clean garments.

“What happens is the CO2 gas turns into a liquid under that kind of pressure,” Bommer said.

Unlike water, Bommer said the liquid CO2 doesn’t leave garments wet in the conventional sense, eliminating the need for a traditional drying process.

Bommer said the process saves about 300 gallons, or more than 1,100 litres, of water per cleaning cycle compared with a conventional wet wash.

Tersus is also preparing to process thousands of shoes for another brand in Canada, while working with several major apparel companies in the United States.

“In Canada we have On shoes. They’re a Swiss company. They just partnered up with us. They’re about to send about 20,000 pairs of shoes to go through the same sort of recommerce process that Lululemon is engaging,” Bommer said.

“In the United States, they work with Arc’teryx, Tersus works with The North Face (and) Canada Goose.”

Canada Goose launched its authenticated Generations resale platform in the United States in January 2023 before expanding it to Canada that July and Japan in 2025. Customers can trade eligible products for a gift card, with pieces authenticated, assessed and prepared for resale.

The company says more than 17,000 products were recirculated through Generations in its first year. In its 2026 fiscal year, more than 19,000 products were recirculated through resale and repair.

“Canada Goose products are built to last, and Generations was created to help extend that journey,” Carrie Baker, president of brand and commercial at Canada Goose, said in a statement.

“We know there’s growing interest in trusted resale, and Generations gives customers an authenticated way to trade in, shop and rediscover Canada Goose pieces that still have years of life ahead of them.”

The trend extends beyond clothing

Ikea Canada has long resold returned and display products through its As-Is departments and in 2019 introduced a program allowing customers to sell eligible used Ikea furniture back to the retailer. The company says it sold 1.6 million products through its Canadian As-Is departments last year and says its resale program continues to grow.

Peter Jones, head of sustainability at Ikea Canada, said customers can check online to see which products are eligible and receive a quote before bringing the furniture to a store in exchange for an Ikea gift card.

“There’s a lot of use cases for this,” Jones said. “A student goes to university. They’re there for three years. They buy a desk and chairs. Maybe at the end of the three years, they don’t want a desk anymore. So then they bring the desk back to us and sell it back to us.”

Jones said he isn’t surprised other major retailers are moving into resale.

“I would suggest that every retailer should be doing this,” he said. “We really would advocate for a circular economy. It’s the only way to have a sustainable business in the long-term.”

Mookerjee said sustainability is another reason brands are increasingly interested in resale, as companies face pressure to demonstrate how they are reducing waste and keeping products in circulation longer.

But he said the appeal of buying used is also changing.

Second-hand shopping can signal that someone is financially savvy or has found something unique, he said, while consumers have become increasingly comfortable with the idea that they don’t have to permanently own everything they use.

“They’re used to kind of acquiring possessions and understanding them as more temporary possessions rather than permanent possessions,” Mookerjee said.

For traditional consignment retailers such as The Peacock Boutique Consignment, the arrival of major brands in a business they’ve occupied for decades is another sign that attitudes toward used goods have changed.

For Wilhelm, there’s also a larger reason to keep clothing circulating.

“I am aware of how damaging the fashion industry is to our planet,” she said. “Just trying to do anything to mitigate that, for the betterment of our planet, is why it’s important to me.”

The post Canadian Debt Hits $3.29 Trillion As Distress Borrowing Surges appeared first on Better Dwelling.
items._ogDesc: Canadian household debt hit $3.29T in July as mortgage growth fell to one of the lowest rates in a generation & distress borrowing climbed.
items.body:
Households are on a borrowing spree, but mortgages are no longer the weapon of choice. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows household credit hit a new high in July. Mortgages continue to represent the lion’s share of debt, but growth is slowing to one of the weakest levels in a generation. Meanwhile, consumer debt continues to outpace mortgages, but for all the wrong reasons.

Canadian Household Total Credit Liabilities Reach $3.29 Trillion

Canadian household debt: total outstanding credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Canadian household debt pushed 0.3% (+$10.0 billion) higher to $3.29 trillion in July, 4.2% (+$131.4 billion) higher than last year. As mentioned, most of it’s still mortgage debt. However, its share is shrinking after consumer credit suddenly made a comeback.

Canadian Mortgage Debt Is Slowing To Unusually Low Levels

Canadian household debt: residential mortgage credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Mortgage debt is cooling, but still growing. The outstanding balance climbed 0.4% (+$8.7 billion) to $2.45 trillion in July, 4.0% (+$93.7 billion) higher than last year. Nearly 4% growth would be considered healthy for a balance this large, but it’s an anomaly for Canada. Over the past 27 years, only 17 months have seen growth at this level or lower. All of those months were in 2023 and 2024, during the recent correction.

Canadian Households Are Tapping Consumer Credit

Canadian household debt: consumer (non-mortgage) credit.

Source: StatCan; Better Dwelling.

Consumer (non-mortgage) credit climbed 0.2% (+$1.3 billion) to $835.7 billion in July, up 4.7% (+$37.6 billion) since last year. The growth rate remains higher than mortgages, and this isn’t one of those good consumer growth surges.

The recent consumer credit bump is due to consumption smoothing and/or distress borrowing, according to TransUnion. Smoothing occurs when households use debt to avoid cutting expenses when their incomes fail to keep up. The credit agency warns that households are tapping higher-interest revolving credit to absorb the higher cost of living. TransUnion also found that mortgages were rising under similar circumstances, as balances are climbing on existing accounts, not new borrowing.

items.title: When a condo closing reveals a much deeper debt crisis
items.description: What brokers should ask before placing the next loan
items.content: <p>What brokers should ask before placing the next loan</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639256039461814791.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: What brokers should ask before placing the next loan
items.body:
The years-long condo market correction in Toronto has seen appraisal challenges hit the headlines, with countless preconstruction buyers suddenly scrambling to make up the difference between the price they originally agreed to pay and the actual amount lenders value the property at.

That’s still a highly prominent problem for the condo sector – but there’s often a much longer story also at play, according to licensed insolvency trustee Paul Franchi, who told Canadian Mortgage Professional appraisal headaches aren’t necessarily where problems began for condo borrowers.

“Picture a father of three working two jobs, supporting rentals that need money every month, with another condo approaching closing,” he said. “There may also be a half-interest in a townhouse bought with a friend. These are not separate investments when the same paycheque is keeping all of them afloat.”

While the mortgage gets paid, groceries might go on a card, with the line of credit growing when another deposit is due. “A long record of on-time payments can sit beside a household that no longer lives within its income,” he said.

Property is increasingly part of the answer when a client arrives with hundreds of thousands of dollars in credit card debt, Franchi said – either because the investments created the shortfall, or because the household was already struggling financially and a big property gain was supposed to fill it.

When the mortgage isn't the real problem

Whatever the case, the appraisal gap may be the final financial problem but not necessarily the only one. Franchi said an important question for brokers whose clients have significant unsecured debt alongside their mortgage is what that unsecured borrowing has been paying for.

“Paying off the cards may help,” he said. “But if the rental shortfalls and household deficit remain, what stops the balances growing again? A rental running at a loss is not automatically an unsuitable investment. Some households can comfortably fund it.

“The problem is relying on steadily expanding credit while waiting for the property to rescue the budget. Private lending can address a temporary need where the repayment plan is credible. The rate alone does not decide suitability – but neither does getting an approval.”

Franchi offered the example of a one-year, interest-only second mortgage for $350,000 at a 10% rate with $44,500 in lender, broker, and legal charges deducted at advance – meaning the client receives $305,500. First-year fees and interest would total about 26% of the net cash received if they come to $79,500, he said, with the $350,000 principal still requiring repayment.

“That loan needs to accomplish something worth its cost,” Franchi said. “A hoped-for rebound is not the same as an executable exit. The broker’s question cannot stop at whether this condo closes. What funds the next 12 months across the household and every property? If the answer remains more borrowing, the conversation needs to widen beyond the next mortgage.”

The other costs of holding on

Another essential step is asking what the property was supposed to do for the household. Sometimes it might have been an investment funded from genuine surplus income; at other times, it might have been expected to produce the gain that would cover another property’s losses and finally put the family ahead. “That is a great deal to ask of one condo,” Franchi said.

“Once someone sees that gain as their way out, letting go is not just accepting an investment loss. It can feel like abandoning the solution to every other financial problem. That’s why the father takes another shift and why the family keeps finding money for a property that never seems to give any back.”

The cost of exiting a contract can also be serious, and Franchi said the contract, full debt picture and a comparison of the available choices are essential. For a consumer proposal meanwhile, insolvency professionals must weigh whether the offer is reasonable and fair to the debtor and creditors, and whether the debtor will be able to perform it.

“Lower unsecured payments may help, but they cannot be treated as permission to keep financing an unaffordable portfolio,” Franchi said. “Sometimes retaining the property works. Sometimes a sale, negotiated exit or bankruptcy needs consideration.

“The aim is a plan the household can carry without depending on a large, timely gain that nobody can promise. Closing the purchase and solving the client’s problem are not necessarily the same thing.”

items._ogDesc: Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.
items.body:
Smartphone apps promising to help shoppers identify Canadian groceries have popped up since the onset of trade tensions with the United States last year.

But how do these apps compare?

After reviewing more than a dozen options, The Canadian Press chose three apps to use on a variety of common grocery items.

Here are the results delivered by Buy Beaver, O SCANada and Maple Scan:

Pied-Mont Dora strawberry jam

Buy Beaver: The jam jar received a full score of 100 because it is manufactured in Quebec. The app didn’t provide information about the parent company or source of ingredients.

Buy Beaver rates items on a scale of zero to 100, which it says is based on the company’s manufacturing location, ingredient sources and the location of its parent company.

O SCANada: Dora was labelled as “Canadian-owned,” as it is a Canadian family-owned food manufacturer headquartered in Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, Que. It didn’t specify the origin of ingredients used to make the jam, which it said was not publicly disclosed.

Maple Scan: Pied-Mont Dora was identified as a Quebec-based company, labelling it as both made and packaged in Canada. It also offers the company’s history, highlighting its Canadian roots.

Kraft peanut butter

Buy Beaver: It scored zero because Kraft Heinz Co. is headquartered in the U.S. The app didn’t recognize its Canadian manufacturing location or source of ingredients.

O SCANada: The app said the product is “not Canadian-owned,” but correctly identified its manufacturing location in Mont-Royal, Que. Meanwhile, ingredient origins aren’t specified. “Origin of peanuts is not publicly disclosed,” the scan found.

Maple Scan: The PB was labelled as both made and manufactured in Canada.

Redpath granulated sugar

Buy Beaver: The sugar scored 70 for being a subsidiary of American Sugar Refining Inc., which it has been since 2007. The app said its manufacturing location is in Canada and that most of its ingredients are Canadian.

Though refined and packaged by Redpath, the majority of sugar cane used in Canadian sugar production is imported in bulk from tropical regions in South and Central America, according to the Canadian Sugar Institute, since Canada’s climate is not suitable for growing sugar cane.

O SCANada: The app called the product “not Canadian-owned,” correctly noting Redpath is a subsidiary of the U.S.-based company. The country of origin for sugar cane was not disclosed. It called the product “not Canadian-owned.”

Maple Scan: The sugar was called a product of Canada, made in Canada and packaged domestically. The app said the manufacturer is based in Ontario and identified American Sugar Refining as its parent company.

French’s tomato ketchup

Buy Beaver: The ketchup earned a score of 70 out of 100, with the app identifying the U.S.-based McCormick & Co. as its owner (McCormick Canada brought its French’s ketchup production in-house in 2021). Manufacturing locations were listed as Canada and Baltimore, Md. It said the ingredients were “100 per cent Canadian.”

O SCANada: The product was labelled “not Canadian-owned,” but knew that its manufacturing plant is in London, Ont. and made with Canadian tomatoes sourced from Ontario growers.

Maple Scan: The app said it is not a product of Canada, but is made in Canada with 100 per cent Canadian tomatoes, and is bottled in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 21, 2026.

items.title: Another huge decision on housing is looming for the government in January
items.description: Policymakers face a big call at the beginning of 2027
items.content: <p>Policymakers face a big call at the beginning of 2027</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639253339698683403.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Policymakers face a big call at the beginning of 2027
items.body:
Geopolitical chaos, rising oil prices, and the US-Canada trade war remain some of the biggest factors currently impacting the national housing market – but the federal government is facing a housing dilemma of another type in the months ahead.

Canada’s ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers, introduced by then-prime minister Justin Trudeau in 2022 and extended for another two years in 2024, is set to expire on January 1, 2027, with no indication yet of whether policymakers plan to extend or scrap the measure.

The policy was first proposed during the 2021 federal election campaign amid the COVID-era housing market boom, when skyrocketing home prices and fierce bidding wars pushed affordability hopelessly out of reach for scores of buyers.

The mortgage industry appears to favour keeping the policy in place, with 58% of respondents to a recent Canadian Mortgage Professional survey indicating they thought it should stay.

But an analysis by law firm Borden Ladner Gervais LLP (BLG) suggested that the government could tweak the ban rather than renewing it outright, citing comments by housing minister Gregor Robertson that offshore capital can still play a role in the national housing market.

Some industry members in favour of adjusting ban

Among the mortgage industry members who favour amending the measure outright is Toronto-based Donaldson Capital mortgage broker and principal Drew Donaldson (pictured below), who said the market should be opened to buyers based in the US.

“I think it should be lifted,” Donaldson told Canadian Mortgage Professional. “Does the US ban Canadians from buying in Florida or Arizona? No, they don’t, and if anything, at least make an exception for our neighbours in the South.”

With Toronto’s condo market still reeling from a years-long slowdown, Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper also believes opening the door to US buyers would be the right move.

She told CMP in February of this year that she favours relaxing or removing the ban on non-resident foreign buyers.

“Look at the Americans that would be very interested in having a second property in Canada, particularly given how they feel about what’s going on in the US,” she said. “Why shouldn’t those people be able to buy a property in Toronto that’s been listed on the market for 18 months?

“It just makes no sense to prohibit that activity, especially now that we have a glut as opposed to a shortage.”

One factor could strongly influence the government in its approach to the issue: namely, the fact that a strong majority of Canadians still support the ban.

Home affordability improved in 10 of 13 major markets last month, according to a new Ratehub.ca analysis, but buyers are still grappling with a challenging outlook across the country thanks to rising interest rates and economic uncertainty.

About 76% of Canadians said they supported the federal foreign buyer ban in a Research Co. poll last year, with no sign that there’s been a significant shift from that consensus in 2026.

What could a revised ban look like?

If the government opts to amend the measure instead of renewing it without a change, the BLG analysis suggested it could look to Australia, which allows some exceptions for purchases by foreign buyers.

Non-resident foreign investors are still permitted to buy vacant land and newbuilds, while purchases for redevelopment supporting the availability of housing on a commercial scale and investments that increase housing stock by more than 20 units are also allowed.

Has the ban worked?

In August, Missing Middle Initiative economist and founding director Mike Moffatt told CTV the ban had had little to no impact on the housing market.

He indicated much of the damage to housing affordability had already been done by the time the measure was introduced in 2022. 

“This was a nationwide rule designed to address problems in two small parts of the country [Toronto and Vancouver],” he said, “and probably came a few years too late to really accomplish much of anything.”

items._ogDesc: This week’s top stories are Canadian real estate’s slum pushes the demand balance to a 29 year low, and mortgage rates are about to rise.
items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada’s Plan To Fix Housing? Just Change What Affordable Means

Back in 2023, the CMHC said that building 3.5 million homes could restore 2004 levels of affordability by 2030. It reiterated the plan a year later, right before the country’s population growth plunged to nearly zero. Combined with the building boom, the bar should have been lower to achieve this goal by 2030. However, the agency’s latest report ignores its previous statement, moving the goalposts. The CMHC now expects affordability will be restored to 2019 levels if roughly 4.4 million homes are built by 2036. If you’re skeptical of the agency’s math, you should be. Here’s a brief overview of why.

Canadian Mortgage Rate Relief Done For This Stage of The Cycle: BMO

One of Canada’s largest banks doesn’t see much relief when it comes to mortgages in the near future. BMO Capital Markets warned the market is now pricing in five rate hikes from the Bank of Canada by the end of 2027. While BMO thinks that may be excessive based on its current read, rate hikes are coming. Mortgages are at cycle low, with hikes expected to throttle home sales in the coming weeks.

Canadian Real Estate Prices Fall, Demand Balance Hits 29-Year Low

The price of a typical home across Canada fell 0.7% to $657,500 in August, marking the third straight monthly drop. The drop was expected with sticky inventory and home sales falling 6.9% to the weakest August since 2012. The combination pushed the demand balance to its lowest level in 29 years. Canada’s housing recovery has barely started, and it’s already facing headwinds.

Canadian Inflation Stalled at 3%, But It’s Higher In All But Two Provinces

The Bank of Canada was lucky enough to see annual growth of CPI stall at 3.0% in August, but most Canadians aren’t that lucky. Only two provinces reported CPI growth at or below 3.0%: BC (+3.0%) and Ontario (+2.4%). Everywhere else came in much higher, especially in Atlantic Canada. The highest price growth was in Nova Scotia (+5.1%), where prices are rising at more than twice the Bank of Canada’s 2.0% target rate.

items._ogDesc: UBCM members say industrial land is critical as businesses diversify markets and seek to boost domestic production
items.body:
Municipalities across B.C. are asking the province to take action to protect and optimize industrial lands as U.S. tariff highlight the importance of “Made in Canada” products.

The majority of mayor and councillors voted in favour of a resolution to protect and optimize industrial lands in the province at the 2026 Union of BC Municipalities convention in Vancouver in Vancouver Friday.

Following the vote, UBCM will put the resolution forward for the province’s consideration.

“We've got generational procurement opportunities right now across the province, nationally and internationally, as we look to diversify markets [away from the U.S.],” said Jason Lum, councillor with the City of Chilliwack and a director at the Fraser Valley Regional District (FVRD), who submitted the motion.

“Whether it be in food processing, in defence, in advanced manufacturing, all of these things require a robust industrial land base.”

Industrial land has been dwindling with only a 10- to 15-year supply remaining in B.C., Lum said. The opportunities to add more land are limited.

He said there are few policies supporting the growth of industrial land and, in some cases, industrial land is being consumed by non-industrial uses. But industrial lands are essential to ensuring a vibrant local economy and providing jobs.

“The province is looking at their Buy BC program, but in order to buy B.C., we need to focus on those sectors that are actively building, creating, manufacturing the goods and producing the goods that we consume,” Lum said.

FVRD and many UBCM members want the province to recognize the importance of industrial lands and provide support to local governments to incentivize its protection. They are also calling for the identification of opportunities to expand the industrial land base.

For example, this could include identifying “brownfield” redevelopment opportunities - sites that have sat vacant and derelict for years - and helping to clean up and redevelop those sites to add more industrial land to the inventory, according to Lum.

“We need to act now, not just to protect and preserve, but also to unlock the incredible potential that we have right now with these generational opportunities that are sitting before us,” said Lum.

items.description: Much anticipated industry event taking place this week (September 24)
items.content: <p>Much anticipated industry event taking place this week (September 24)</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639253554174790721.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Much anticipated industry event taking place this week (September 24)
items.body:
Canada's biggest dedicated gathering for women in the mortgage industry is arriving this week, an unmissable event offering a full day of networking and educational opportunities.

The Women in Mortgage Summit Canada takes place on Wednesday, September 24, at the International Centre in Toronto, Ontario. Hosted by Canadian Mortgage Professional (CMP), the one-day leadership event is built for brokers, lenders, executives, and emerging professionals who want substantive content, structured networking, and direct conversation about what it takes to build a lasting career in this market. 

The summit carries pre-approval from Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) for 3.25 continuing education (CE) units in the Professional Development Category for 2026. For brokers managing licence renewal obligations, that designation alone makes attendance worth considering. 

Previous editions of the summit have sold out, with the 2025 event welcoming over 600 attendees. 

A keynote built around one career, honestly told

The opening keynote at 8:55 a.m. features Rola Dagher, a transformational leadership speaker and former president and chief executive officer of Cisco Canada.

Dagher came to Canada as a young refugee with no English and no formal education, started in Bell's telemarketing department, and ended up as President and CEO of Cisco Canada and Global Channel Chief at Dell Technologies. 

Her session is structured around a three-part leadership framework, applicable whether an attendee is two years or twenty into a career, covering what resilience looks like in a difficult market, and why developing other women in the industry is both the right thing and the strategically sound thing to do.

Leah Zlatkin, chief operating officer of Mortgage Outlet Inc. in Toronto, chairs the day and delivers welcome and closing remarks.

Behind every strong mortgage market are organizations driving confidence, efficiency, and expertise. We're proud to recognize our partners at #WomenInMortgageCA Summit 2026!

Register: https://t.co/L0jfVYZt75 pic.twitter.com/UWclMPHlKs — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) September 9, 2026

What the sessions cover

Three Power Panels run across the day. The first, held at 8:55 a.m., cuts directly into the market conditions brokers are managing right now: tariffs, rate uncertainty, a renewal wave reshaping client books, and buyers who are hesitating for reasons that have little to do with rates and everything to do with fear.

Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres, and Michele Steko, vice president of national broker relations at Sherwood Mortgage Group, are among the panellists. 

The second panel examines the leadership patterns that lead to burnout — specifically, how the dependability and hands-on approach that builds early careers can, if unchecked, become the habits that grind professionals down.

Sofia Hondrogiannis, associate vice president of national distribution and broker services at TD Bank, and Elena Robinson, vice president of residential sales at First National Financial LP in Canada, join the panel.

The third panel, in the afternoon, is focused on client communication: what to actually say when clients tell you they're waiting, how to stay connected after funding in a way that builds loyalty and referrals, and how to talk about life events — not just rates — so clients think of you first when things change. 

Jamie Doolittle, head of BMO BrokerEdge, is on that panel. Doolittle is also among CMP's Top 50 Women of Influence in mortgage for 2026, a list that recognised 50 leaders across the full breadth of Canada's mortgage sector this year.

An AI workshop at 1:00 p.m. covers real tools and workflows mortgage professionals are already using — in client communication, file preparation, follow-ups, and marketing — alongside a direct conversation about compliance, data privacy, and the risks of cutting corners.

The session is led by Dalia Barsoum, founder of Streetwise Mortgages and co-founder of Wisely AI Technologies, whose brokerage has funded more than $2 billion in real estate mortgages. 

A fireside chat in the late afternoon turns to long-term business questions: succession planning, building systems that reduce owner dependency, and navigating major life disruptions — from illness to ownership transitions — without losing the business underneath you.

Part of a two-day industry event

This year, Women in Mortgage Summit Canada is part of MortgageFest Canada, which means a summit pass includes full access to Canada's biggest mortgage event on both days — more content, more connections, the whole industry in one place.

MortgageFest Canada runs September 23 and 24 at the same venue, with a speaker lineup that signals where the Canadian broker industry is heading over the next two years.
